דלא שכיחי אנשים הרב בעל שב יעקב חלק א"ע סימן ג' כתב אילו לא דמסתפינא לומר נגד הרמב"ם הייתי אומר דנשים כשרות להעיד מדינא דהא בב"ק דקתני המשנה בני חורין ובני ברית (עיין אורים) וקעביד הגמרא צריכת' דעבדים ל"ל חייס וגוים אינו בני מצות הא אשה דיש לה חייס והיא בכלל מצות מעידה. ולא ידעתי מה זה דחידש הלא דברים אלו אמורים כהווייתן בתרומת הדשן סי' שנ"ג במקומו דיש פתחון פה לומר כן אבל דחה אותו. והאמת דאף הרמב"ם לא אמרה אלא דלכך נאמרה במשנה לדחות לב הטועים אבל ח"ו לומר במסקנ' דאשה כשרה ואם כן הא דתנן שבועת עדות אינה נוהגת בנשים הא נוהגת בנזקין ויש עלי' קרבן שבועה וגם הא דעבד פסול הוא מק"ו דאשה וגזלן ואם אשה כשרה נימא דיו אלא ברור דפסולה והא דלא קתני במשנה ג"כ למעט נשים (עיין ביש"ש דמשמע דמפרש הא דקתני והנשים בכלל הנזק היינו למעט עדות נשים לנשים ע"ש ולא ידעתי מנ"ל זה) משום דאין נשים שכיחי בארוות סוסי' וח"ו שיהיו נשים במקום משכן גוים ועבדים הפרוצים וכ"כ הוא בעצמו ונכון:
urim_vetumim_tumim.en:
A woman is disqualified. Rambam writes in Hilchot Edut 9:2 that women are disqualified from testimony, as Scripture says, "by the mouth of two witnesses," using the masculine form and not the feminine. Kesef Mishneh asks why Rambam omitted the Gemara's proof from "the two men shall stand," which refers to witnesses: men and not women. He also asks how Rambam can prove anything from masculine language, since the Torah generally speaks in the masculine. The difficulty is substantial, but Rambam's wording can be explained precisely. The Yerushalmi asks in another context: if the Torah already speaks of two goats, why repeat "two"? It answers that the repetition teaches they should be alike. So too here, if the Torah could simply say "witnesses," why specifically say "two witnesses"? The word "two" is therefore extra and can be expounded. Since it is written in masculine form, it teaches two male witnesses, not two female witnesses. This removes the objection that Torah generally speaks in masculine language. Here the number word itself is unnecessary. Still, one may ask that the extra word "two" is needed to exclude minors. The Gemara derives from "men" and not minors. But why is a verse needed for minors if they lack full legal understanding? The answer is that minors are believed in certain matters, such as identifying a father's handwriting. Chazal relied on them because in matters not requiring great intellectual judgment they possess a lesser degree of understanding. Without an explicit exclusion, one might therefore have thought that in Torah matters of similarly limited factual complexity a minor could also testify together with an adult. Certainly we would never have thought that two minors alone could establish Torah testimony, because even in rabbinic matters we do not rely upon them alone. The possible novelty would only be that a minor could join an adult. Scripture therefore says "two," requiring both witnesses to be of equal testimonial standing. Once "two" excludes a minor from joining an adult, the word "men" becomes available to exclude women. Alternatively, if "men" excludes minors, then the extra masculine "two" excludes women. Either way, women are excluded. This also clarifies the Gemara's question whether "the two men shall stand" refers perhaps to the litigants. At first glance that seems impossible, because there would be no reason to exclude women from being litigants. But according to what I have explained, the natural first use of "men" is to exclude minors, as in many Torah passages. If the verse concerned litigants, it could teach that a minor is not a full litigant, consistent with the rule that one does not take an oath on a minor's claim. The Gemara therefore proves from "those who have the dispute" that the litigants are already mentioned separately, so "the two men" must refer to the witnesses. Then the combined wording necessarily excludes both minors and women. Thus Rambam's formulation is exact: "men" can exclude minors, while "two" excludes women. His words are carefully grounded.
Where men are not commonly present. Shev Yaakov, Even HaEzer part 1, siman 3, writes that were he not hesitant to dispute Rambam, he would say women are legally valid witnesses. He argues from the Mishnah in Bava Kamma that specifies free persons and members of the covenant. The Gemara explains the need for each category: slaves lack lineage and non-Jews are not bound by mitzvot. A woman has lineage and is bound by mitzvot, so perhaps she should be valid. I do not know what novelty this adds. Terumat HaDeshen siman 353 already raises exactly this possibility and rejects it. Certainly one cannot conclude that women are valid. If so, the Mishnah that the oath of testimony does not apply to women would be wrong in damage cases where women could testify. Likewise the Gemara derives a slave's disqualification by a kal vachomer from woman and robber. If a woman were valid, that derivation would collapse. Rather, women are plainly disqualified. Why then does the Mishnah in Bava Kamma not explicitly add women to its exclusions? Because women are not ordinarily present in stables and similar locations involving unruly slaves and non-Jews. It would have been improper and uncommon for them to be there. This is also essentially Shev Yaakov's own explanation, and it is correct.

urim_vetumim_urim.he:
אשה פסולה דכתיב אנשים ולא נשים ועיין ע"ש בתומים שכתבתי בישוב דברי הרמב"ם:
אפי' במקום דלא שכיחי וכו' כן מפרש הרמב"ם בפי' המשנה וכ"כ ת"ה דקתני בב"ק בני חורין ובני ברית למעט עבדים וגוים דהא דהעמידו התנא שם ולא במקום אחר דלא תימא במקום נזקין בארוות סוסי' ועדרות צאן לא שכיחי אלא אלו וקמ"ל דמ"מ פסולים ע"ש:
וכל זה מדינא כו' הקשה הסמ"ע לקמן בסי' ת"ח הביאו לשון הרמב"ם דבניזקין אינם נאמנים לא עבדים ולא כיוצא בהן אף דלא שכיחי שם כשרים ולא הגיהו לא מחבר ולא רמ"א דמתורת תקנה נאמנים כי הך דהכא ותי' דנזיקין שכיחי משא"כ כאן מילי דאקראי פי' במלתא דשכיחי לא עשו תקנה זו כי כל איש עושה עול ישכיר גוים ופסולים להעיד שחבירו הזיקו ולא שבקית חי' לכשרים כ"כ ת"ה סי' שנ"ג ע"ש:
כגון בב"ה של נשים וכו' ומהרש"ל ביש"ש פ"ק דבב"ק העלה דאם החזיק במקום שם ג"ש אין מועיל עדות נשים להוציא ע"פ מחזקתו וכן ע"א כשר נאמן יותר מב' נשים ע"ש ש"ך:
או קרוב ומהרש"ל כתב להעיד לטובת קרובו לא יעיד דחם ללבו בראו' שקרובו מוכה ואין נותן ללב להבחין מי המתחיל ודעתו קרובה לקרוב שלו ע"ש ואפשר מהרש"ל לשיטתו דס"ל כמש"ל ריש סי' ל"ג דשונא גדול שחבירו רוצה להורגו וכדומה אף לדידן דקי"ל כחכמים פסול ומזה הוסיף בדבר תקנה אפילו קרובו מוכה אינו יכול להעיד אבל לפי מש"ל דקרובי מוכה יכולים להעיד א"כ בתקנה זו אין הבדל כמ"ש מהרי"ק:
והוא שתובע טוען ברי אבל אם הוא בעצמו א"י רק עפ"י העדים הללו תובעו לא מהני עדותן וע"ש במהרי"ק סי' צ"ג משמע עפ"י ע"א מפסולים הללו אבל בשני עדים לא נזכר שם ואפשר דרמ"א היה מדמה אותן להדדי והבו דלא לוסיף בכלל התקנה:
urim_vetumim_urim.en:
A woman is disqualified. For the verse states "men," excluding women. See Tumim, where I explained Rambam's words.
Even in a place where qualified witnesses are not commonly found, etc. Rambam explains the Mishnah this way, and Terumat HaDeshen likewise explains the Mishnah in Bava Kamma that requires witnesses to be free persons and members of the covenant, excluding slaves and gentiles. The Mishnah stated this specifically there lest one think that in cases of damage occurring around horse stables or flocks, where only such persons are commonly present, they should be accepted. It teaches that they remain disqualified. See there.
All this is the strict law, etc. Sema asks that below, in siman 408, the Mechaber cites Rambam's ruling that in damages neither slaves nor similar persons are believed even where qualified witnesses are not commonly present, and neither the Mechaber nor Rama adds that by enactment they may be believed as here. He answers that damages are common, whereas the present cases are occasional. In a common matter the Sages did not institute such a relaxation, because otherwise every wrongdoer could hire gentiles or otherwise disqualified persons to testify that his fellow caused damage, and no property would remain secure for qualified people. So writes Terumat HaDeshen, siman 353.
Such as in the women's section of the synagogue, etc. Maharshal in Yam Shel Shlomo, Bava Kamma, chapter 1, concludes that if a person has maintained possession of a place there for three years, testimony of women does not suffice to remove him from that possession. Likewise, one qualified witness is more credible than two women. Shach.
Or a relative. Maharshal writes that a person should not testify for the benefit of his relative, because when he sees his relative being struck his emotions are aroused and he may fail to distinguish who began the altercation, since his inclination favors his relative. See there. Perhaps Maharshal follows his own view, mentioned above at the beginning of siman 33, that an intense enemy, such as one whose fellow seeks to kill him, is disqualified even according to the Sages. On that basis he extends the enactment here and holds that even a relative of the person being struck cannot testify. But according to what I wrote there, that relatives of the person being struck may testify, there is no distinction under this enactment, as Maharik writes.
Provided that the claimant asserts a definite claim. If the claimant himself does not know what occurred and brings the claim only on the basis of these witnesses, their testimony is ineffective. See Maharik, siman 93, where this appears to be stated concerning one such disqualified witness. Two such witnesses are not mentioned there, and perhaps the Rama equated the cases. In any event, one should not extend the enactment beyond its stated scope.
